title: Access Token Manipulation: Create Process with Token
shortTitle: Access Token Manipulation: Create Process with Token
summary: Creating a process with a token means launching an entirely new program under an access token that was not issued to the caller, so the new process runs from its first instruction with the privileges and group memberships of a different account. Windows offers supported entry points for this, including process creation interfaces that accept an existing token and the interactive runas command, which builds a fresh logon session from credentials. The token can come from a duplicate of a live process token or from a newly created logon session, which is why this behaviour is often chained with the other token sub-techniques. The activity leaves three useful signals: a process creation record whose assigned user does not match the parent session, a preceding logon session event that produced the token, and a process image whose path and command line may be legitimate while its identity is not. Legitimate administration produces the same pattern, because support tools and scheduled tasks start work as another account on purpose, so the discriminator is a mismatch between the account, the host and the role that account normally performs, especially when the new process immediately touches sensitive files or starts network connections.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker starts a brand new program while pretending to be a different user. The program carries that other user pass from the moment it starts. It is different from borrowing a pass for one small worker inside an existing program, because here a whole new program is launched.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers often need a long running program, so a copied pass alone is not enough. Starting a new program under another identity gives them a stable tool with strong rights. The program file itself may be a normal Windows tool, so file scanning finds nothing wrong. Only the identity and the logon behind it give the game away.
howItWorks: The attacker needs a pass, either copied from a running program or made from known credentials.
A Windows function starts a new program and is given that pass to use.
The new program begins with the rights and group memberships of the other account.
It can read protected files, change settings or start network connections as that user.
The command runas does something similar, but it asks for the user password first.
Logs show a new process whose user does not match the session that launched it.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where a cleaner finds a manager key card and copies it. Instead of just opening one store room, the cleaner uses the copied card to start a cleaning machine that runs all night. The machine carries the manager card, so every door it reaches opens. The hotel log shows a normal machine doing normal work, but under the manager name.
takeaways: A whole new program runs as another account, which gives the attacker a stable foothold.
The executable may be a harmless system tool, so identity matters more than the file name.
Compare each new process account with the account that started it and with normal job roles.

objectives: Explain how a new process can be started with an access token taken from another account.
Describe how this differs from attaching a stolen token to a thread in an existing process.
Recognise the logon session event that must occur before a process is created with a token.
Explain how the runas command relates to this behaviour and why it needs credentials.
Judge when process creation under another account is normal administration instead of abuse.
